body.heading: 'Just because' is the whole point
paragraphs: Most calls to grandparents have a reason attached: a birthday, a question, a problem. The calls that land differently are the ones with no agenda at all — five minutes because it is Tuesday and their voice was wanted. Elders can tell the difference instantly.
Short and frequent beats long and rare. A regular ten minutes every week becomes part of the furniture of both lives; the annual hour-long call requires an occasion and a warm-up.

body.heading: Give children the phone
paragraphs: A grandchild's call is an event in a grandparent's week out of all proportion to its length. Let children make their own calls, with their own news: the lost tooth, the match, the joke they are currently telling everyone. Prompt them with one question to ask in return — about the grandparent's week, garden, or childhood — and conversations stop being reports.
Video helps the very young and the very old, who both do much of their communicating with faces and showing things. A drawing held up to a camera is a complete sentence.

body.heading: Ask for the stories while you can
paragraphs: Sprinkle in the questions only they can answer: what was your street like, what did your mother cook, what was your first job. Record them if they are willing — a phone on the table is enough. Families rarely regret having asked; they often regret the timing.
If distance or hearing makes calls hard, letters and voice notes carry the same warmth and can be kept. A grandparent's story in their own voice is a family treasure with a play button.

description: Short, frequent calls with no agenda — and children making their own — keep grandparents woven into ordinary family life.
